In summary, our research is concerned with

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed cluster mass function in the LMC is consistent with the predictions of a simple model in which the clusters lose mass by evaporation at a constant rate, and that the observed cluster age distribution is consistent with the model of mass-independent disruption, which is also the model that best explains the observed M-tau distribution.
the observed g(M,tau) distribution of clusters in the Magellanic and Antennae systems, as well as in the Milky Way, is consistent with the simple mass-independent disruption model.
the observed cluster populations in the LMC and SMC are best explained as the result of mass-independent gradual disruption, and that the dominant disruption mechanism is evaporation.« less
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found a good, first order description for the disruption of young star clusters, and that the dominant disruption process is the same in the Magellanic clouds as in the merging Antenae galaxies, and possibly also in elliptical galaxies.

we are able to show the following: (1) the mass functions of young and old star clusters in the Magellanic clouds are different, (2) the mass function of young clusters is a power-law and that of old clusters is peaked at a mass M = 10{sup -2} M{sun} (3) the observed bivariate distributions of masses and ages for young star clusters in the LCM and SMC can be explained by a model with gradual mass independent disruption,

the mass-dependent disruption model for star clusters fails, and the mass-independent disruption model works well for star clusters in the Luminous and Ultra-Luminous Infrared Galaxies, the Magellanic and the Antennae galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the observed distribution of star clusters as a function of mass and age is consistent with a simple model for the disruption of clusters.

, in the Magellanic clouds, the disruption of star cluster is not mass dependent, at least not in the mass range 10{sup -2} M{sup -3} M{sup sun} (M{sub sun} is the solar mass) and age range of 10{sup {minus}3} to 10{sup +8} yr.
the mass function for young clusters in galaxies like the LMC is a power law, and the mass function for ancient globular cluster populations is peaked.
